Posted May 14, 2004
Analysis by Richard Cowan sponsored by Advanced Nutrients

During the time that I have been analyzing prohibitionist propaganda on MarijuanaNews, it has become obvious how the process works, but the latest barrage was more thorough than most. (Consequently, it was very pleasant to find that The Lancet, the UK's great medical journal has not joined the Gadarene rush.)

It all began with a typically off-the-wall statement by John Walters, the Drug Czar, prohibitionism's chief ideologist (think of Wolfowitz in wolf's clothing.) He actually went to Miami to warn Hispanic youth about the dangers of BC Bud.
See
Bush Should Have John Comical Ali Walters Explain The Iraq War, Then The Media Would Never Ask Any Embarrassing Questions. Doctrine Of Drug Czar Infallibility? Blame Canada, Again.

Of course, Walters knew what was in the propaganda pipeline. On April 20th (4/20. Get it?), The National Center on Addiction and Substance Abuse (CASA) at Columbia University issued a rehash of their 1999 rehash, Casa Report Finds More Teens in Treatment for Marijuana than for Alcohol or All Other Illegal Drugs Combined. Huge Increase in Emergency Room Admissions Among 12 to 17 Year Olds Where Marijuana is Implicated. Non-Medical Marijuana II: Rite Of Passage Or Russian Roulette?
From 1999 see
Califano Says, " Teens who smoke marijuana are playing a dangerous game of Russian roulette. " And Other Brilliant Insights

The only surprising thing about CASA reports is that Columbia University continues to prostitute itself by allowing CASA to trash any semblance of academic standards. (The CASA Board of Directors is made up of blue-chip names who are conned into accepting CASA at face value because of its association with Columbia. CASA is headed by Joe Califano.)
See
Califano And Friends Lie To Us About Marijuana And Holland -- the Mfiles
and
The AP Gives Califano A Free Ride For Prohibitionist Propaganda
and
PseudoSurvey Of the Week Shows 4 Times As Many 12 Year Olds Drink As Smoke Marijuana, But That Is Not the Spin
and
How the Prohibitionist Funding Racket Really Works Shown As Califano Shills for DEA and NIDA.

The CASA reports pretend to be new research when they are actually just cribbed from the standard prohibitionist party line as pushed by NIDA and the Drug Czar's office. A Columbia student who tried to do this would get kicked out of school.

For example, the press release announcing the latest version says, More kids are in treatment for marijuana dependence and abuse than ever before, and marijuana is a culprit in an increasing proportion of emergency room visits.

The 1999 version headlined, More Teens " Nearly 88,000 -- in Treatment for Marijuana Than Any Other Drug Including Alcohol.

However, the claims about Emergency Room data were not new then. In Marijuana Myths, Marijuana Facts, Zimmer and Morgan cite a 1995 claim by then HHS Secretary Donna Shalala saying, In 1993, twice as many kids ended up in emergency rooms for marijuana use as for heroin and cocaine combined. (Appropriately, that was in the Wall Street Journal, which would attack any other sort of lie that Shalala might tell, but welcomed her lies about marijuana.)
See
Shalala Says That Parents Are Wrong To Be Relieved
That Their Children Are Using Marijuana Instead Of Heroin!
Survey Results From California Do Not Support Party Line, So They Are Buried.

Of course, the text of the CASA report uses the correct term, mention when it claims that it also found that emergency department mentions of the drug among 12- to 17-year olds jumped 48 percent since 1999.

The substantive point is that the mention of a substance does not necessarily have anything to do with the reason for the ER visit. The data in question is based on mentions of up to six substances by a visitor to an emergency department. Alcohol is included in this data only when it is in combination with an illegal drug, nonetheless alcohol in combination mentions totaled over 207,000.

CASA knew what it was doing when it said that marijuana was the culprit.
See
Cannabis Prohibition Prostitutes Science In New Emergency Dept. Data. Hiding the Truth Behind A Cloud of Lies.

It has now been at least nine years since the media started falling for this easily checked misuse of data. There were over 113,000 mentions of marijuana in 2002, but only 32,000 were marijuana-only mentions, and even then marijuana was not necessarily the cause of the visit. To put this into context, there were over 100 million emergency room visits in 2002. Benzodiazepines tranquilizers like Valium accounted for over 105,000 mentions,
From http://dawninfo.samhsa.gov/pubs_94_02/pickatable/2002/2.2.0.xls

But cases involving alcohol, which are not covered in this data set, totaled over 25 million! 32,000 for marijuana; 25 million for alcohol. But CASA wants to warn everyone about the dangers of marijuana!

The next sentence in the CASA press release then claims, Especially troubling is the possibility that this rise in teen emergency department mentions is related to the increased potency of the drug.
See
Dan Forbes Documents Walters Lies About Potency. Understanding That The War On Cannabis Is Built On Lies Is Key to Understanding More Than Just Drug War.

It is at this point that the connection with the Drug Czar's Florida blather becomes obvious.

However, the most egregious lie in the CASA report has to be their misrepresentations of The Institute of Medicine's 1999 report, Marijuana and Medicine: Assessing the Science Base.
See
Executive Summary Of The IOM Report, Marijuana And Medicine: Assessing The Science Base

The IOM report trashed the gateway theory, but CASA tries to give the impression that it supports it. In fact, Califano was so outraged by the IOM's conclusion that he wrote an Op-ed in the Wall Street Journal (of course) in which he defended the Gateway theory against the IOM report.
See
The Wall Street Journal Responds To The IOM Report
By Having Califano Defend The " Gateway Theory "

He complained, The Institute of Medicine study fails to discuss mounting scientific evidence that children who smoke pot are much likelier to use drugs like cocaine, heroin and LSD.

Now CASA tries to create the impression that the IOM report supported this gateway theory by quoting it in a way as to create the impression that it supports Califano:
" The association between the use of marijuana and other drugs is well established: most current cocaine and heroin users have already used marijuana, and people who use marijuana are at higher risk for using other illegal drugs. The Institute of Medicine's 1999 report, Marijuana and Medicine: Assessing the Science Base, states: Not surprisingly, most users of other illicit drugs have used marijuana first. In fact, most drug users begin with alcohol and nicotine before marijuana--usually before they are of legal age. In the sense that marijuana use typically precedes rather than follows initiation of other illicit drug use, it is indeed a gateway drug.

The IOM report also undermined CASA's claims about marijuana addiction. The IOM report said, " A distinctive marijuana withdrawal syndrome has been identified, but it is mild and short-lived. The syndrome includes restlessness, irritability, mild agitation, insomnia, sleep EEG disturbance, nausea, and cramping. "
See
Is marijuana addictive?

Most outrageously, the CASA report also misrepresents the IOM report's conclusions on the medical use of cannabis, claiming, As the Institute of Medicine's 1999 report, Marijuana and Medicine: Assessing the Science Base, indicates, the risks and benefits of medical marijuana are matters for physicians, scientists, the National Institutes of Health and the Food and Drug Administration to address. These issues should not be resolved by referenda; pharmaceutical prescription is a matter for physicians, not politicians.

The IOM said no such thing. On the contrary, the report flatly stated that " There is no clear alternative for people suffering from chronic conditions that might be relieved by smoking marijuana, such as pain or AIDS wasting. "

If Columbia University has any intellectual standards at all, it will do its own study of the CASA report and then invite them to move elsewhere.

Perhaps, CASA could affiliate itself with JAMA, the Journal of the American Medical Association. They seem quite happy to be used as a prohibitionist propaganda outlet.

The May 5th, 2004 edition carried a NIDA-funded article, PREVALENCE OF MARIJUANA USE DISORDERS IN THE UNITED STATES 1991-1992 AND 2001-2002 that was pure party line prohibitionist propaganda. (NIDA funds 85% of all studies on illicit drugs.)
See
Institute of Medicine Report on Medical Marijuana Contradicts Assumptions for NIDA Monkeyshines. Special to MarijuanaNews
and
How NIDA Made Monkeys of the Media. 4 Primates Are News; 4 Million People Are Not. Analysis by Richard Cowan

Amazingly, the JAMA article says, Increases in the prevalence of marijuana use disorders were most notable among young black men and women and young Hispanic men. Although rates of marijuana abuse and dependence did not increase among young white men and women, their rates have remained high. The results of this study underscore the need to develop and implement new prevention and intervention programs targeted at youth, particularly minority youth.

Inasmuch as being forced into treatment by the courts is considered by the DSM-IV as proof that treatment is necessary, and blacks and Hispanics are arrested disproportionately, one might wonder if this is not a circular argument, but no!
See
Walters Tells a New Lie. Oh Happy Day! People Need Treatment If They Are Sent to Treatment, By Definition. And How Do They Treat Marijuana Addicts? We Couldn't Make This Up, But They Did.

In the present context, it necessarily means that we need to arrest more young blacks and Hispanics, which will of course put more in treatment which will prove that we need to arrest more young blacks and Hispanics.

If the JAMA complains that they never mention the word arrest well, precisely! They do not take responsibility for the state violence that they advocate.
See
Calling All Quacks: The Therapeutic Police State and the Politicization of Medicine. Doctors Cannot Study The Violence of Cannabis Prohibition. Because They Are The Disease, Not The Cure.

Instead, the JAMA says that the concomitant increase in potency of delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol ( delta 9-THC ) may have contributed to the rising rates.

That must mean that the inferior races are more easily hooked than us white folk. Of course, they did not quite put it that way, but this is obviously racist claptrap that will have an effect as pernicious as any specifically racist laws.
See
Prohibition and The Prison State. Protecting Youth and Minorities. In DEAland, The UK and France Prisons Are Full.

The Lancet upholds its standards.

Press release:

Authors of a study conclude that more evidence is required to determine the nature and extent of the association between cannabis use and negative psychosocial outcomes.

Issue 15 May 2004
(pp 1568, 1579)
Lancet 2004; 363: 1568, 1579-88

Authors of a study in this week's issue of THE LANCET conclude that more evidence is required to determine the nature and extent of the association between cannabis use and negative psychosocial outcomes.

The use of cannabis and other illicit drugs by young people is linked to psychosocial harm including psychological health problems, the use of other illegal drugs, reduced educational attainment, and antisocial behaviour. However, whether these associations are causal (ie, cannabis use is a direct cause of psychological illness and antisocial behaviour) remains unclear.

John Macleod from the University of Birmingham, UK, and colleagues reviewed general population longitudinal studies reporting associations between illicit drug use by young people and psychosocial harm. They identified 48 relevant studies, of which the most reliable evidence came from 16 studies.

In general, consistent associations were identified between cannabis use and both lower educational attainment and increased reported use of other illicit drugs. Less consistent associations were found between cannabis use and psychological health problems and problematic behaviour.

Dr Macleod comments: " Despite widespread concern, we have found no strong evidence that use of cannabis in itself has important consequences for psychological or social health. This finding is not equivalent to the conclusion that use of cannabis is harmless in psychosocial terms; problems with the available evidence render it equally unable to support this proposition. Better evidence is needed in relation to cannabis, which is widely used, and in relation to other drugs that, although less widely used, might have important effects ".

In an accompanying Commentary (p 1568) Franjo Grotenhermen from the Nova-Institut GmbH, Germany, states: " There is some reason to believe that cannabis contributes to psychosocial problems in adolescents and young adults, and no responsible adult would want young people to take drugs. There is no question that this issue is an important candidate for education and prevention, but there is a fierce debate on the place repressive measures should have in this context. There is little reason to believe that criminalisation has had a strong effect on the extent of cannabis use by young people. Moreover, prohibition itself seems to increase the harmfulness of drug use and cause social harm. By stopping all cannabis users from being treated as criminals, I believe this year's change by the British Government of its cannabis law (a declassification from class B to C) is a sensible attempt to balance the possible harms caused by cannabis and its prohibition... we must learn to deal with drugs and their possible dangers without fear ".

Excerpt From The Lancet:

Psychological and social sequelae of cannabis and other illicit drug use by young people: a systematic review of longitudinal, general population studies
By John Macleod, Rachel Oakes, Alex Copello, Ilana Crome, Matthias Egger, Mathew Hickman, Thomas Oppenkowski, Helen Stokes-Lampard, George Davey Smith

Summary

Background Use of illicit drugs, particularly cannabis, by young people is widespread and is associated with several types of psychological and social harm. These relations might not be causal. Causal relations would suggest that recreational drug use is a substantial public health problem. Non-causal relations would suggest that harm-reduction policy based on prevention of drug use is unlikely to produce improvements in public health. Cross-sectional evidence cannot clarify questions of causality; longitudinal or interventional evidence is needed. Past reviews have generally been non-systematic, have often included cross-sectional data, and have underappreciated the extent of methodological problems associated with interpretation.

Methods

We did a systematic review of general population longitudinal studies reporting associations between illicit drug use by young people and psychosocial harm.

Findings

We identified 48 relevant studies, of which 16 were of higher quality and provided the most robust evidence. Fairly consistent associations were noted between cannabis use and both lower educational attainment and increased reported use of other illicit drugs. Less consistent associations were noted between cannabis use and both psychological health problems and problematic behaviour. All these associations seemed to be explicable in terms of non-causal mechanisms.

Interpretation

Available evidence does not strongly support an important causal relation between cannabis use by young people and psychosocial harm, but cannot exclude the possibility that such a relation exists. The lack of evidence of robust causal relations prevents the attribution of public health detriments to illicit drug use. In view of the extent of illicit drug use, better evidence is needed.

Lancet 2004; 363: 1579-88
